 \section{Discussion}
 \label{sec:discussion}
-\enlargethispage*{6\baselineskip}
 
 \subsection{Temporal DIF as Structured Signal}
 \label{sec:disc_temporal}
 
 \looseness=-1
-Temporal DIF detects \emph{that} items function differently across cohorts, not \emph{why}---and this is by design. The signal is structured: stratifying by model type reveals opposite patterns---base models ($N{=}1{,}409$) are 60.1\% reference-favoring with a strong difficulty gradient ($\rho = -0.570$), while instruct models ($N{=}478$) are 65.6\% focal-favoring with a near-zero gradient ($\rho = -0.079$; $\chi^2 = 562.7$, $p < 10^{-124}$). This reversal cannot arise from a single mechanism, validating DIF as a meaningful diagnostic regardless of underlying cause. Detailed mechanism analysis---exclusion arguments, difficulty--direction interactions, and mixed-mechanism semi-synthetic validation---appears in \Cref{app:mechanism_discussion}.
+Temporal DIF detects \emph{that} items function differently across cohorts, not \emph{why}---and this is by design. Stratifying by model type reveals opposite patterns: base models ($N{=}1{,}409$) are 60.1\% reference-favoring ($\rho = -0.570$), while instruct models ($N{=}478$) are 65.6\% focal-favoring ($\rho = -0.079$; $\chi^2 = 562.7$, $p < 10^{-124}$). Following the impact-bias framework~\citep{camilli1994methods}, this reversal reflects structured item-level bias rather than uniform group impact, validating DIF as a mechanism-agnostic diagnostic (\Cref{app:mechanism_discussion}).
 
 \looseness=-1
-Item-level DIF matters even when aggregate rankings are preserved ($\rho \approx 0.997$): it reveals \emph{which} capability dimensions shift---diagnostic value that aggregate scores mask. DIF-ordered removal shows ranking degradation accelerates with instability (\Cref{app:fig_rho_degradation}); among the top 3.8\% most displaced models, 33.6\% of pairwise rankings reverse (\Cref{app:rank_reversal}).
+Composition downsampling ($\Delta = 1.08$\,pp), base-only (32.1\%), and instruct-only (36.5\%) temporal analyses independently confirm DIF is not an artifact of cohort structure (\Cref{app:composition_control,app:baseinst_temporal,app:within_arch}). These findings have immediate implications for leaderboard maintenance: temporal DIF means the same score carries different meaning across model generations, motivating periodic psychometric audits alongside score reporting.
 
-\looseness=-2
-Within-family analysis validates matching: Llama-2 vs.\ Llama-3 raw C\% $= 61.3\%$ reflects the ability gap ($d = -0.99$); after nearest-neighbor matching, C\% drops to $28.3\%$, consistent with temporal matched C\% ($28.9\%$), confirming that DIF captures structured item-level change beyond ability differences.
+\looseness=-1
+Three features distinguish LLM temporal DIF from educational settings: (1)~the observed C\% (13.5--29.2\%) substantially exceeds typical educational DIF rates~\citep{clauser1998dif}; (2)~DIF flags and web-overlap labels are near-independent (Jaccard $= 0.206$), unlike educational settings where DIF correlates with construct-irrelevant variance; (3)~model families introduce non-independence (design effect) absent in human testing, necessitating DEFF correction (\Cref{app:deff}).
 
 \subsection{Recommended DIF Audit Protocol}
 \label{sec:disc_protocol}
 
 \looseness=-1
-Item-level properties do not predict DIF susceptibility (AUROC $= 0.60$; \Cref{app:predictive}), precluding pre-screening. We recommend MH-DIF audits whenever ${\geq}$500 models accumulate ($K{=}3$ suffices for smaller corpora; \Cref{tab:k3_power}), with action levels calibrated to $\rho$-degradation (\Cref{app:fig_rho_degradation}). DIF removal is least disruptive (\Cref{app:fig_downstream}), motivating equating~\citep{kolen2014equating,habba2026growingpains}.
+Item-level properties do not predict DIF susceptibility (AUROC $= 0.60$; \Cref{app:predictive}), precluding pre-screening. We recommend MH-DIF audits whenever ${\geq}$500 models accumulate ($K{=}3$ for smaller corpora; \Cref{tab:k3_power}), with action thresholds calibrated to $\rho$-degradation (\Cref{app:fig_rho_degradation}). Flagged items warrant mechanism-conditional responses: DIF $\times$ web-overlap co-occurrence warrants removal; DIF on web-clean items is inconsistent with contamination as sole mechanism (annotate; DIF alone cannot determine causation); base/instruct direction reversal motivates refined cohort definitions. DIF-corrected scoring motivates equating adjustments~\citep{kolen2014equating,habba2026growingpains}.

 \section*{Limitations}
 
 \looseness=-1
-Three primary limitations apply. (1)~The semi-synthetic framework uses uniform binary response flipping, a worst-case injection model; reported $\Delta\mathrm{TPR}$ values are upper-bound estimates, and detection power under realistic contamination patterns (partial memorization, format-specific advantages) is untested. The framework detects measurement changes but does not attribute causal mechanisms; follow-up expert review is needed to determine whether flagged items should be retired or retained. (2)~The MH $\chi^2$ test assumes independent examinees; LLM model families violate this assumption. Three convergent corrections (${\approx}$27--29\%) and family-level cluster bootstrap (95\% CI: $[26.7\%, 53.2\%]$) bound the impact, but the extreme relatedness of some families (e.g., hundreds of Llama-2 fine-tunes) exceeds the clustering levels studied in educational settings~\citep{french2010hierarchical}. (3)~Cross-subject matching assumes contamination affects a minority of domains; $\Delta\mathrm{FPR}$ rises to 0.069 when contamination spans ${\geq}20$ subjects. Temporal cohorts defined by calendar year provide coarse granularity, and generalizability to open-ended or partial-credit benchmarks is untested. Multidimensional DIF~\citep{ackerman1992didmf} may arise when MMLU's 57 subjects span distinct latent dimensions; cross-subject matching mitigates between-domain multidimensionality but not within-domain violations. IRT parameters are used only for auxiliary power analysis; all core DIF results are nonparametric.
+Three primary limitations apply. (1)~The semi-synthetic framework uses uniform binary response flipping, a stylized injection model; reported $\Delta\mathrm{TPR}$ values may overestimate detection power, and detection power under realistic contamination patterns (partial memorization, format-specific advantages) is untested. The framework detects \emph{that} items function differently but not \emph{why}---a deliberate design choice that limits immediate actionability; follow-up expert review is needed to determine whether flagged items should be retired or retained. (2)~The MH $\chi^2$ test assumes independent examinees; LLM model families violate this assumption. Two DEFF estimators (13.5--29.2\%) and family-level cluster bootstrap (95\% CI: $[26.7\%, 53.2\%]$) bound the impact, but the extreme relatedness of some families (e.g., hundreds of Llama-2 fine-tunes) exceeds the clustering levels studied in educational settings~\citep{french2010hierarchical}. (3)~Cross-subject matching assumes contamination affects a minority of domains; $\Delta\mathrm{FPR}$ rises to 0.069 when contamination spans ${\geq}20$ subjects. Although composition control experiments show a small residual shift ($\Delta = 1.08$\,pp; \Cref{app:composition_control}), base/instruct ratio changes between cohorts remain a potential confound that cannot be fully eliminated without single-architecture longitudinal data. Temporal cohorts defined by calendar year provide coarse granularity, and generalizability to open-ended or partial-credit benchmarks is untested. Multidimensional DIF~\citep{ackerman1992didmf} may arise when MMLU's 57 subjects span distinct latent dimensions; cross-subject matching mitigates between-domain multidimensionality but not within-domain violations. IRT parameters are used only for auxiliary power analysis; all core DIF results are nonparametric. Additionally, model release dates need not align with training-data cutoff dates, and generalization beyond MCQ-format benchmarks requires further validation, though GSM8K (open-ended) shows consistent patterns.

 The choice of matching variable (the total score used for stratification) affects both validity and interpretation. We distinguish three matching strategies: (1)~\emph{standard matching} uses the within-benchmark total score on all items of the same benchmark; (2)~\emph{cross-subject matching}, adapting purified subtest matching~\citep{swaminathan1990logistic} to the LLM multi-subject setting, uses the total score on all subjects \emph{other than} the one containing the item under test, preventing the matching variable from absorbing injected contamination signals (\Cref{sec:injection}); and (3)~\emph{external matching} uses the total score on a different benchmark entirely (e.g., MMLU total score as the matching variable when testing DIF on GSM8K items), providing an independent ability proxy uncontaminated by the target benchmark. Cross-subject and external matching both address matching variable contamination but at different granularities: cross-subject operates within a multi-domain benchmark, while external operates across benchmarks. Total score matching is sufficient: IRT $\theta$ correlates at $r = 0.9986$ with total scores (\Cref{sec:structural}).
 
-\paragraph{LLM-specific challenges.} Applying MH-DIF to LLMs introduces assumptions absent in educational testing. First, overlapping training corpora violate local independence; permutation simulation confirms LD-attributable FPR inflation $< 0.001$~pp under cross-subject matching (\Cref{app:method_details}). Second, fine-tuned variants and merges within model families are not independent examinees; graduated de-duplication shows family structure does not inflate C\% (\Cref{sec:structural}). Third, bimodal ability distributions (base vs.\ instruction-tuned) motivate quintile-based rather than parametric stratification. Fourth, MMLU's 57-subject structure raises a multidimensionality concern: if 2023 and 2024 cohorts differ on secondary ability dimensions, total-score matching may produce spurious DIF~\citep{ackerman1992didmf,roussos1996multidimensionality}. We address this through three lines of evidence: (i)~domain-level ability profiles are nearly flat across cohorts (Cohen's $d$: STEM $= 0.26$, Humanities $= 0.16$, Social Science $= 0.15$, Other $= 0.15$; range $= 0.12$), indicating uniform improvement that total-score matching adequately captures; (ii)~cross-subject and within-subject matching show strong agreement ($\kappa = 0.80$, 5 subjects, 834 items; the 20\% discordance is distributed across domains rather than concentrated in specific subjects), with cross-subject matching yielding 2.7\,pp more C items---an upper bound on any multidimensional confound; (iii)~cross-subject-unique C items do not concentrate in subjects with large cohort ability shifts, further dissociating multidimensional confound from the observed DIF signal (\Cref{sec:structural,app:structural}). Unlike standard purified MH that conditions on total test score, we match on cross-subject total score to avoid criterion contamination when target-subject items themselves may be compromised---an adaptation specific to multi-domain LLM benchmarks where subjects may be differentially affected.

 \label{sec:related_work}
 
 \paragraph{Contamination Detection.}
-A growing family of methods detects benchmark contamination through model behavior or training data analysis. Membership inference approaches estimate whether a model has seen specific items during training: Min-K\% \citep{shi2024mink} and Min-K\%++ \citep{zhang2024minkpp} use token-level log-likelihood statistics, while Time Travel \citep{golchin2024timetravel} probes models with temporal cues and \citet{oren2024proving} prove contamination through exchangeability tests. Performance-based detectors identify contamination through statistical anomalies \citep{dekoninck2024constat,liang2026dvd,tao2026selfcritique,deng2024investigating}. \citet{balloccu2024leak} provide a broader taxonomy of leakage detection strategies. These methods share a common validation practice: they verify detection accuracy against web-overlap or n-gram labels \citep{li2024contamination} that classify items based on verbatim matches in publicly accessible corpora. Such labels measure \emph{global exposure} (whether an item exists in training data) rather than \emph{differential item functioning} (whether an item behaves differently across model cohorts). This global-vs-differential distinction motivates our ground truth analysis (\Cref{sec:groundtruth}). Work on LLM memorization \citep{carlini2022quantifying, tirumala2022memorization} establishes that memorization depends on data frequency and model scale, reinforcing the distinction between global exposure and differential behavior. \citet{wang2026fragility} show that existing contamination detectors are fragile under reinforcement learning, further motivating behavioral approaches grounded in psychometric theory.

 \paragraph{IRT in LLM Evaluation.}
-IRT adoption in LLM evaluation has accelerated: \citet{lalor2019irt} introduced IRT to NLP, \citet{vania2021irt} assessed test set discriminability, and \citet{rodriguez2021evaluation} demonstrated that not all evaluation examples are equally informative. Recent extensions include PSN-IRT \citep{zhou2026psnirt} for benchmark quality at scale, TinyBenchmarks \citep{maiapolo2024tinybenchmarks} for IRT-based item selection, scalability coefficients for detecting bad benchmark items \citep{hardy2026scalability}, IRT-based evaluation quality~\citep{kraus2024irt}, ATLAS \citep{li2025atlas} for computerized adaptive testing of LLMs, and competency-focused IRT evaluation in medical domains \citep{luo2025medirt}. The closest concurrent work is Growing Pains \citep{habba2026growingpains}, which uses IRT calibration to establish anchor items for cross-temporal score equating via fixed-parameter calibration \citep[FPC;][]{kim2019fpc}. While Growing Pains prescribes how to equate scores after instability is detected, our work diagnoses \emph{which} items exhibit instability and quantifies its magnitude---the diagnostic step that must precede equating. Their anchor-item selection can directly consume our stable-item set as pre-screened candidates; our finding that 31\% of items exhibit temporal DIF identifies which items should \emph{not} serve as anchors. To our knowledge, no prior work applies DIF to benchmark temporal comparability---contamination detection and psychometric evaluation optimization have developed as separate threads.

103	-The Mantel-Haenszel procedure for DIF detection was introduced by \citet{holland1988mh} and remains the most widely used method in educational testing due to its simplicity and well-characterized statistical properties \citep{clauser1998dif}. Alternative approaches include logistic regression DIF \citep{swaminathan1990logistic}, SIBTEST \citep{shealy1993sibtest}, Lord's $\chi^2$ test \citep{lord1980irt}, and the Raju area method \citep{raju1988area}; \citet{millsap1993dif}, \citet{zumbo1999handbook}, and \citet{penfield2007dif} provide comprehensive reviews. DIF analysis is a specific instance of measurement invariance testing \citep{meredith1993invariance, vandenberg2000invariance, millsap2011invariance}, which examines whether a measurement instrument functions equivalently across populations. MIMIC models offer a latent-variable approach to the same problem \citep{muthen1985mimic, woods2009mimic}, and \citet{teresi2007dif} reviews DIF methods across applied domains. Cross-subject matching---computing the stratification variable from domains other than the one being tested---has psychometric precedent in the DIF literature \citep{nandakumar1993dif,donoghue1993mh}; our adaptation addresses LLM-specific challenges of multi-domain local dependence and simultaneous contamination control at scale. We do not modify the MH procedure; our contribution is the application context and the empirical findings it reveals. The 5,227-examinee scale exceeds typical DIF applications~\citep{belzak2020smallsample}. The impact-versus-DIF confound is addressed through matched-ability quintile analysis, IRT $\theta$-conditioning (as sensitivity check), and a random-split control (\Cref{sec:temporal}).
104	+The Mantel-Haenszel procedure for DIF detection was introduced by \citet{holland1988mh} and remains the most widely used method in educational testing due to its simplicity and well-characterized statistical properties \citep{clauser1998dif}. We retain the standard MH statistic and develop LLM-specific adaptations around it: cross-subject matching for contamination control (with a formal $\Delta\mathrm{FPR} = 0$ guarantee), DEFF correction for non-independence, and semi-synthetic validation absent ground-truth labels. The impact-versus-DIF confound is addressed through matched-ability quintile analysis, IRT $\theta$-conditioning (as sensitivity check), and a random-split control (\Cref{sec:temporal}).

106	 \paragraph{Benchmark Quality and Design.}
107	-Several concurrent approaches address benchmark reliability from complementary angles. The Benchmark Health Index~\citep{zhu2026bhi} and Benchmark$^2$~\citep{qian2026benchmark2} perform meta-evaluation of static benchmark quality at a single snapshot; our temporal DIF analysis diagnoses \emph{when} measurement properties shift. MMLU-CF~\citep{zhao2025mmlucf} reconstructs contamination-free items, and MMLU-Pro~\citep{wang2024mmlupro} extends item difficulty; DIF monitoring provides a lower-cost alternative when reconstruction is infeasible, identifying which existing items remain measurement-invariant rather than replacing them. Combined with the prescriptive equating framework of Growing Pains~\citep{habba2026growingpains} (discussed above), these approaches span the full lifecycle from diagnosis (our work) to reconstruction~\citep{zhao2025mmlucf} to calibration~\citep{habba2026growingpains}. \citet{maeda2025difllm} predict which item features associate with DIF in educational settings; we instead detect DIF empirically across LLM cohorts at scale. Dynamic benchmarks \citep{kiela2021dynabench, li2024latesteval, white2025livebench} and self-evolving update frameworks~\citep{ying2024automating,xu2025benchmark} mitigate contamination by construction, yet none provides psychometric equating across versions. Leaderboard rankings are sensitive to minor evaluation perturbations~\citep{alzahrani2024benchmarks}. Broader surveys \citep{chang2024survey, burnell2023rethink} identify benchmark saturation and item-level opacity as systemic challenges that our DIF analysis directly addresses.
108	+Meta-evaluation of static benchmark quality~\citep{zhu2026bhi,qian2026benchmark2} assesses quality at a single snapshot; our temporal DIF analysis diagnoses \emph{when} measurement properties shift. MMLU-CF~\citep{zhao2025mmlucf} reconstructs contamination-free items and MMLU-Pro~\citep{wang2024mmlupro} extends item difficulty; DIF monitoring identifies which existing items remain measurement-invariant without replacement. \citet{maeda2025difllm} use LLMs to predict DIF in human assessments---the reverse direction; we apply DIF to LLM benchmarks with models as examinees.  \section{Discussion}
 \label{sec:discussion}

 \subsection{Temporal DIF as Structured Signal}
 \label{sec:disc_temporal}
 
 \looseness=-1
-Temporal DIF detects \emph{that} items function differently across cohorts, not \emph{why}---and this is by design. The signal is structured: stratifying by model type reveals opposite patterns---base models ($N{=}1{,}409$) are 60.1\% reference-favoring with a strong difficulty gradient ($\rho = -0.570$), while instruct models ($N{=}478$) are 65.6\% focal-favoring with a near-zero gradient ($\rho = -0.079$; $\chi^2 = 562.7$, $p < 10^{-124}$). This reversal cannot arise from a single mechanism, validating DIF as a meaningful diagnostic regardless of underlying cause. Following the impact-bias framework~\citep{camilli1994methods}, this reversal reflects structured item-level bias rather than uniform group impact, validating DIF as a mechanism-agnostic diagnostic (\Cref{app:mechanism_discussion}).

These findings have immediate implications for leaderboard maintenance: temporal DIF means the same score carries different meaning across model generations, motivating periodic psychometric audits alongside score reporting.
 
-\looseness=-2
-Within-family analysis validates matching: Llama-2 vs.\ Llama-3 raw C\% $= 61.3\%$ reflects the ability gap ($d = -0.99$); after nearest-neighbor matching, C\% drops to $28.3\%$, consistent with temporal matched C\% ($28.9\%$), confirming that DIF captures structured item-level change beyond ability differences.

+Three features distinguish LLM temporal DIF from educational settings: (1)~the observed C\% (13.5--29.2\%) substantially exceeds typical educational DIF rates~\citep{clauser1998dif}; (2)~DIF flags and web-overlap labels are near-independent (Jaccard $= 0.206$), unlike educational settings where DIF correlates with construct-irrelevant variance; (3)~model families introduce non-independence (design effect) absent in human testing, necessitating DEFF correction (\Cref{app:deff}).
 
 \subsection{Recommended DIF Audit Protocol}
 \label{sec:disc_protocol}
 
 \looseness=-1

We recommend MH-DIF audits whenever ${\geq}$500 models accumulate ($K{=}3$ suffices for smaller corpora; \Cref{tab:k3_power}), with action levels calibrated to $\rho$-degradation (\Cref{app:fig_rho_degradation}).  \section*{Limitations}
 
 \looseness=-1
-Three primary limitations apply. (1)~The semi-synthetic framework uses uniform binary response flipping, a worst-case injection model; reported $\Delta\mathrm{TPR}$ values are upper-bound estimates, and detection power under realistic contamination patterns (partial memorization, format-specific advantages) is untested. The framework detects measurement changes but does not attribute causal mechanisms; follow-up expert review is needed to determine whether flagged items should be retired or retained. (2)~The MH $\chi^2$ test assumes independent examinees; LLM model families violate this assumption. Three convergent corrections (${\approx}$27--29\%) and family-level cluster bootstrap (95\% CI: $[26.7\%, 53.2\%]$) bound the impact, but the extreme relatedness of some families (e.g., hundreds of Llama-2 fine-tunes) exceeds the clustering levels studied in educational settings~\citep{french2010hierarchical}. (3)~Cross-subject matching assumes contamination affects a minority of domains; $\Delta\mathrm{FPR}$ rises to 0.069 when contamination spans ${\geq}20$ subjects. Temporal cohorts defined by calendar year provide coarse granularity, and generalizability to open-ended or partial-credit benchmarks is untested. +Three primary limitations apply. (2)~The MH $\chi^2$ test assumes independent examinees; LLM model families violate this assumption. (3)~Cross-subject matching assumes contamination affects a minority of domains; $\Delta\mathrm{FPR}$ rises to 0.069 when contamination spans ${\geq}20$ subjects. Although composition control experiments show a small residual shift ($\Delta = 1.08$\,pp; \Cref{app:composition_control}), base/instruct ratio changes between cohorts remain a potential confound that cannot be fully eliminated without single-architecture longitudinal data. 1	\section{Discussion}
2	\label{sec:discussion}
3	
4	\subsection{Temporal DIF as Structured Signal}
5	\label{sec:disc_temporal}
6	
7	\looseness=-1
8	Temporal DIF detects \emph{that} items function differently across cohorts, not \emph{why}---and this is by design. Stratifying by model type reveals opposite patterns: base models ($N{=}1{,}409$) are 60.1\% reference-favoring ($\rho = -0.570$), while instruct models ($N{=}478$) are 65.6\% focal-favoring ($\rho = -0.079$; $\chi^2 = 562.7$, $p < 10^{-124}$). Following the impact-bias framework~\citep{camilli1994methods}, this reversal reflects structured item-level bias rather than uniform group impact, validating DIF as a mechanism-agnostic diagnostic (\Cref{app:mechanism_discussion}).
9	
10	\looseness=-1
11	Composition downsampling ($\Delta = 1.08$\,pp), base-only (32.1\%), and instruct-only (36.5\%) temporal analyses independently confirm DIF is not an artifact of cohort structure (\Cref{app:composition_control,app:baseinst_temporal,app:within_arch}). These findings have immediate implications for leaderboard maintenance: temporal DIF means the same score carries different meaning across model generations, motivating periodic psychometric audits alongside score reporting.
12	
13	\looseness=-1
14	Three features distinguish LLM temporal DIF from educational settings: (1)~the observed C\% (13.5--29.2\%) substantially exceeds typical educational DIF rates~\citep{clauser1998dif}; (2)~DIF flags and web-overlap labels are near-independent (Jaccard $= 0.206$), unlike educational settings where DIF correlates with construct-irrelevant variance; (3)~the near-independence admits two interpretations: DIF captures a broader signal---including capability evolution and training methodology shifts---of which contamination is one component, or DIF and contamination detection measure distinct constructs. The base/instruct direction reversal and model-type interaction (OR $= 4.75$; \Cref{app:mechanism_discussion}) favor the former, as contamination alone cannot explain opposing DIF patterns. Either interpretation supports periodic DIF audits.
15	
16	\subsection{Recommended DIF Audit Protocol}
17	\label{sec:disc_protocol}
18	
19	\looseness=-1
20	Item-level properties do not predict DIF susceptibility (AUROC $= 0.60$; \Cref{app:predictive}), precluding pre-screening. We recommend MH-DIF audits whenever ${\geq}$500 models accumulate ($K{=}3$ for smaller corpora; \Cref{tab:k3_power}), with action thresholds calibrated to $\rho$-degradation (\Cref{app:fig_rho_degradation}). Flagged items warrant mechanism-conditional responses: DIF $\times$ web-overlap co-occurrence warrants removal; DIF on web-clean items is inconsistent with contamination as sole mechanism (annotate; DIF alone cannot determine causation); base/instruct direction reversal motivates refined cohort definitions. DIF-corrected scoring motivates equating adjustments~\citep{kolen2014equating,habba2026growingpains,suk2026rethinking}.

Interesting. The k distribution data shows that contamination is pervasive — 54/57 subjects show contamination evidence, with median prevalence 39.8%. This actually cuts both ways:
